title: Early Indigenous Presence / Paleoindian Period (c. 10,000-8000 BCE)
summary: Rare fluted stone points connect Long Island to Indigenous life at the end of the last Ice Age while also showing how much the surviving archaeological evidence cannot answer.
content:
Earliest Archaeological Evidence

The earliest widely accepted archaeological evidence of people on Long Island dates to the end of the last Ice Age, roughly 12,000 to 10,000 years ago. Rare fluted projectile points associated with the Paleoindian period have been reported from Brooklyn eastward to Riverhead. Most were surface finds rather than objects excavated from intact layers, so their exact setting and use cannot be reconstructed.1

Stone, Movement, and Knowledge

Several fluted points were made from local quartz or quartzite, materials that are difficult to shape predictably. Others were made from chert, chalcedony, or jasper not naturally available on Long Island. Together they document skilled work with local stone and connections beyond the island.2

Lower sea levels exposed a broader coastal plain south of present-day Long Island. That changing post-glacial landscape shaped travel and access to water, plants, animals, and stone. Archaeology does not support a precise picture of clothing, household organization, population size, or diet for Long Island's earliest inhabitants, and no local fluted point has been found in direct association with mammoth or mastodon remains.3

Deep Indigenous History

These rare objects are evidence of Indigenous life and knowledge more than ten thousand years ago. They belong to the deep history of Native Long Island, even when the surviving archaeological evidence cannot identify a particular community name or reconstruct a complete way of life.

References

  • John A. Strong, The Algonquian Peoples of Long Island from Earliest Times to 1700 (1997), pp. 35-38.
  • Walter Saxon, 'The Paleo-Indian on Long Island' (1973), reprinted in The Coastal Archaeology Reader (1978), pp. 251-261.
  • Gaynell Stone, ed., The History & Archaeology of the Montauk (1993), p. 604.
why_this_matters: The earliest archaeological finds extend Indigenous Long Island history beyond written records by more than ten thousand years. They also show the limits of archaeology: a few displaced stone points cannot supply a complete account of the people who made and used them.
